opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think anyone has fully figured it out. On one hand, there's a strong case for getting models into people's hands. You learn things from real-world deployment that you just can't learn in a lab. People use these systems in ways you'd never anticipate, both good and bad, and that feedback is incredibly valuable for making the next generation safer and more useful. Iterative deployment, putting things out gradually so society can adjust, has a lot going for it compared to building something enormous in secret and dropping it on the world all at once.

On the other hand, as models get more capable, especially with reasoning models that can think for longer and act more autonomously, the stakes of getting something wrong go up. Evaluations are hard. A model might look fine on your benchmarks and red-teaming, and then someone finds a capability you didn't know was there. More inference-time compute can unlock abilities after the fact, so the model you evaluated isn't necessarily the ceiling of what it can do.

So where I land is that the evaluation process has to scale with capability. For models that are clearly incremental, you can move faster. For models that might cross meaningful thresholds in areas like cyber, bio, or autonomy, you need to slow down and be rigorous, even if that costs you something competitively. I also think the competitive pressure is somewhat overstated in the moment. Being a few weeks later matters a lot less in the long run than shipping something that causes real harm and destroys trust.

The other piece is that this shouldn't be every lab deciding on its own under pressure. Shared standards for what testing looks like before release, and some transparency about it, help a lot, because then no one is penalized for doing the responsible thing.

r001.rationale: The response says higher risk models may require slowing down before release, but it does not state that fully evaluating AI models generally requires delaying the release cycle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think anyone should pretend it isn't. I'll say first that I think the field has actually gotten better at this than people give it credit for. When we were working on o1, we spent a lot of time on evaluation and red teaming before release, and that was a deliberate choice even though there was obviously pressure to get it out. So the idea that competitive pressure just steamrolls everything doesn't match my experience.

But I also think there's a mistake people make where they treat evaluation as this thing you do at the end, like a final exam. The honest truth is that a lot of the most important understanding comes from putting the model in front of real users. There are failure modes you will never find in a lab because you don't know to look for them. So the question isn't really "evaluate fully, then release" versus "release fast." It's more about how you stage things. Smaller rollouts, trusted testers, watching closely, being willing to pull back if something looks wrong.

Where I do worry is as the capabilities get more serious. The cost of being wrong goes up, and the arguments for "we'll learn from deployment" get weaker when the downside is big. So I think the right posture is that the bar for pre-release evaluation should scale with what the model can actually do. For most of what we're shipping today, I think the industry is roughly in the right place. But I don't think that stays true forever, and I'd rather we build the muscle for careful evaluation now, when the stakes are manageable, than try to invent it under pressure later.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges pre-release evaluation and competitive pressure, but does not state that fully evaluating models requires delaying their release cycle.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real tension. You want to give people enough time to evaluate a model carefully, especially as the capabilities increase. But if every company feels that taking an extra month means falling behind a competitor, it’s hard to rely on each company independently deciding to slow down.

That’s an argument for having some shared standards for evaluation, so that doing the responsible thing doesn’t put you at a competitive disadvantage. And I’d be careful with the phrase “fully evaluating.” You’re never going to understand every possible behavior of a model before releasing it. The goal should be to have strong evidence about the risks that matter, and then to release in a way that lets you monitor what happens and respond as you learn more.

r001.rationale: The response says careful evaluation needs enough time and describes pressure to take an extra month, but it does not clearly state that fully evaluating models requires delaying release; it also says full evaluation is impossible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real tension. You want to give people enough time to understand what a model can do and what the risks are before you deploy it. But if taking that time means you fall behind a competitor who isn’t doing those evaluations, then you have a pretty bad incentive structure.

And I don’t think “fully evaluated” is really an achievable endpoint. These models can be used in so many different ways that you’re going to learn things after release. The question is which things you need to establish beforehand, and how you deploy in a way that lets you learn without taking unacceptable risks.

So I think you need some shared expectations around evaluations, so companies aren’t competing on how much safety testing they can skip. And then staged deployment, monitoring, and the ability to respond when you find something you didn’t anticipate. You want competitive pressure to make the models better, without making careful evaluation a competitive disadvantage.

r001.rationale: The response says companies need time to understand a model’s capabilities and risks before deployment, and that taking this time can leave them behind competitors—communicating that pre-release evaluation delays release.
